author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The spotted lanternfly has spread to more than 150 Massachusetts cities and towns, and state officials now say the focus is shifting from eradication to management, New England Public Media reported Monday.

The invasive insect feeds on the sap of trees and woody plants. It also favors tree-of-heaven, another invasive species that is common in urban areas and can help the lanternfly establish new populations.

Massachusetts officials say the pest can threaten agricultural resources, including grapevines. Researchers and growers are working on identification, monitoring and treatment, while the state continues watching areas that do not yet have confirmed infestations.

The insects can spread when egg masses attach to vehicles, outdoor equipment and other surfaces. Residents are encouraged to inspect cars, clothing and belongings before moving them from infested areas.

State recommendations include reporting sightings in areas believed to be free of the pest, along with using approved treatments and crop netting where appropriate. Officials say biological-control research is promising but remains years away from broad use.
dek: State officials say Massachusetts is shifting from trying to eradicate spotted lanternflies to managing their impact on crops, trees and vineyards.
headline: Spotted lanternfly spreads across more than 150 Massachusetts communities
